reasons: The lake identity record gives case_name_full as Preston v. United States, court as U.S. Supreme Court, date_decided as 1964-03-23, and year as 1964.
The lake citations record lists official citation 376 U.S. 364, parallel citations 84 S. Ct. 881 and 11 L. Ed. 2d 777, and vendor-neutral citation 1964 U.S. LEXIS 1578.

The opinion squarely discusses search incident to arrest: "when a person is lawfully arrested, the police have the right, without a search warrant, to make a contemporaneous search of the person of the accused".

The lake treatment scope note identifies Preston as a SITA case, supporting placement on a search-incident-to-arrest home; the 1964 date and pre-Chimel doctrinal framing support the limited Historical role.
residual_risks: No separate SIA Persons page or role taxonomy is disclosed, so the role label is verified only from the opinion's subject matter, the lake scope note, and the case date.

reasons: The opinion repeatedly frames the search as a motorcar search and cites Carroll and Brinegar before asking whether an exception to the warrant rule applies.
The lake scope note expressly treats Preston as cross-doctrinal to the later automobile-exception line, stating that Chambers and Michigan v. Thomas distinguish Preston rather than overrule it.
The opinion states: "Once an accused is under arrest and in custody, then a search made at another place, without a warrant, is simply not incident to the arrest."

On the vehicle facts, the opinion states that the car was searched after the arrestees were taken to the station and the car towed to a garage, then concludes: "the search was too remote in time or place to have been made as incidental to the arrest" and the warrantless search was unreasonable.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Keep the holding tied to search-incident justification, not to all warrantless vehicle searches.
